analysis.one_liner: Requires health plans that cover addiction treatment to apply the same limits and cost-sharing as for other medical care.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have barred health plans from charging higher copays or imposing tighter visit limits on drug and alcohol treatment than on other care, was referred to the Senate Health Committee in March 2001 and never received a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required private health plans that cover substance abuse treatment to treat it like any other medical care: the same deductibles, copays, day and visit limits as for medical and surgical benefits. It applied to group and individual plans from employers with more than 25 workers and took effect in 2002. Plans would not have been forced to add addiction treatment coverage, only to stop treating it as a second-class benefit when they offered it. The bill was sent to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee and died there.
analysis.who_benefits: People with drug or alcohol addiction and their families, who today often face much higher copays, stricter day limits, and lower annual or lifetime caps on addiction treatment than on other care. Also addiction treatment providers, whose services would become covered on equal terms.

how_it_helps.text: Bars health plans from imposing treatment limits or cost requirements (deductibles, coinsurance, cost-sharing, annual or lifetime dollar caps) on substance abuse treatment benefits unless similar limits apply to medical and surgical benefits [S3].
Covers the full range of care: inpatient detoxification, residential treatment, outpatient counseling and medication management, and prevention services [S3].
Applies to both employer group plans and individual market coverage, effective January 1, 2002, and does not override state laws offering stronger protections [S3].
Exempts employers with 25 or fewer employees, shielding the smallest businesses from added costs [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and the employers with more than 25 workers who sponsor their plans, which would bear higher claims costs when addiction treatment is covered on par with other care. Those costs would partly flow back into premiums, and some plans could respond by dropping the addiction benefit altogether, since the bill does not require offering it.

drawbacks.text: The bill does not require plans to offer substance abuse treatment at all; it only applies if a plan voluntarily covers it, so a plan could comply by dropping the benefit rather than equalizing it [S3].
Higher claims costs for insurers and larger employers would likely be passed on as higher premiums for everyone in those plans, including people who never use addiction treatment [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real: ending the practice of treating addiction coverage as a lesser benefit makes treatment reachable for people who need it. The bill's own carve-outs blunt it, though: plans can avoid the mandate by not offering the benefit, and small employers are exempt. Costs to plans are modest by design, but the escape hatch means the guarantee is weaker than it looks.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced on March 22, 2001, sent to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, and the committee never acted on it; no vote ever happened in either chamber.

narrative.text: Senator Paul Wellstone introduced the bill with Senate Majority Leader Tom Daschle and Senator Daniel Inouye on March 22, 2001 [S1].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the same day [S5].
No further action was ever taken; the bill died in committee when the 107th Congress ended in January 2003 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and large employers were better off because the bill died, since they avoided a requirement to equalize addiction treatment coverage and its costs. People with substance abuse disorders got nothing.

for.name: Sen. Paul Wellstone
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it on the Senate floor.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Judd Gregg (R-NH)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral; it never received a markup or a vote.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had only Democratic sponsorship (all 4 cosponsors were Democrats), and the Republican-chaired committee never acted on it, so no formal vote ever revealed how the parties lined up.

industries.note: Plans that cover substance abuse treatment would have had to match its deductibles, copays, and visit limits to those for regular medical care, raising claims costs. They could have escaped by dropping the benefit entirely, since the bill does not require offering it.

industries.industry: Addiction treatment providers (detox, residential, and outpatient programs)
industries.note: Equal coverage terms would remove financial barriers that keep patients out of their programs, expanding demand for inpatient, residential, and outpatient services.

industries.industry: Large employers (25+ workers) sponsoring health plans
industries.note: They would absorb higher health benefit costs, partly passed through premiums, though the smallest employers were exempt.
